data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for the better-corroborated theory is defensible on his own terms as a non-inductive methodological rule of 'risk-minimization' rather than a probabilistic prediction; it costs the agent the assurance of future success, accepting instead that they are choosing the theory that has proved most resilient to error so far, without assuming this resilience guarantees future performance.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the preference implicitly assumes that the conditions making Theory A superior in the past will hold in the future, it collapses into induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the definition of 'verisimilitude' used to justify the preference relies on a logical formalism that Tich\u00fd and others have proven inconsistent.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If acting on a theory inherently requires assigning it a higher subjective probability of success, thereby smuggling in Bayesian assumptions.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'justification' (which requires induction to assert future truth) and 'criticism' (which uses past failures to eliminate error-prone options). By preferring the theory that has survived the severest tests, the scientist selects the option with the highest known informational content and the lowest known falsity, treating the preference as a strategic bet on the current state of knowledge rather than a prophecy of nature's uniformity.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
